title: Grouped data and sampling quiz
description: Ten questions drawn at random from a bank of thirteen, covering the estimated mean, modal and median classes, the estimated range, and fair sampling. A calculator is allowed.

questions.prompt: What is the midpoint of the class $135 \le m < 140$?
Amounts spent by 25 children: 35 dollars: 2 children, 40 dollars: 4, 45 dollars: 7, 50 dollars: 9, 55 dollars: 3. Calculate the mean amount spent.
questions.explanation: $\Sigma fx = 70 + 160 + 315 + 450 + 165 = 1160$ and $\Sigma f = 25$, so the mean is $1160 \div 25 = 46.40$ dollars. (These are exact values, not classes, so this mean is exact.)

questions.prompt: Heights: $150$–$160$ cm: 6, $160$–$170$ cm: 10, $170$–$180$ cm: 4. Estimate the mean height.
Why is a mean calculated from a grouped frequency table only an estimate?

options.text: We use midpoints because the exact values are not known
Because the frequencies might be wrong
Because the mean is always rounded
It is not an estimate — it is exact

questions.explanation: Grouping hides the exact values, so each class is represented by its midpoint.

questions.prompt: Times: $15 \le t < 19$ is the first class and $35 \le t < 39$ is the last. Estimate the range.
Distances: $0$–$1$ km: 10, $1$–$2$ km: 15, $2$–$3$ km: 7, $3$–$4$ km: 2, $4$–$5$ km: 1. What is the modal class?
questions.explanation: The highest frequency, 15, is in $1 \le d < 2$.

questions.prompt: For the same 35 students, which class contains the median distance?
questions.explanation: The median is the 18th value. Running totals are 10, 25, … so values 11 to 25 are in $1 \le d < 2$.

questions.prompt: There are 60 values in a grouped table. In which position is the median?
Regrouping the same data into different classes can change the modal class.
questions.explanation: True. The modal class depends on how the classes are chosen, not only on the data.

options.text: Population figures from a government website
Your own stopwatch timings of classmates running 100 m
A newspaper's table of football results
A tally chart you filled in by counting cars

questions.explanation: Secondary data was collected by someone else: the website and the newspaper. The other two you collected yourself, so they are primary.

questions.prompt: To find out what films people like, Tom asks the first 50 people into a cinema. 38 are men. What is the main problem?

options.text: The sample is unintentionally biased towards men's opinions
50 people is far too many
Film preference is quantitative data
There is no problem

questions.explanation: Tom did not mean to, but his sample over-represents men, so the results may not reflect everyone's views.

questions.prompt: Match each variable to its type.
questions.explanation: Descriptions (eye colour, country) are qualitative. Numbers (a time, a count) are quantitative.

questions.prompt: Which is the best survey question?

options.text: How many hours of TV do you watch on a school night? 0–1 / 1–2 / 2–3 / more than 3
Don't you think you watch too much TV?
Do you watch TV?
How much TV do you watch?

questions.explanation: a is neutral, specific (school nights, hours) and has clear options. b is leading, c gives almost no information, and d is too vague.
